sections.html:
Monroeville is a home rule municipality east of Pittsburgh in Allegheny County, with 28,640 residents in 2020 and an estimate of 27,685 for 2025. The population has been flat to slightly down since 1980, so most houses sit in established neighborhoods and many were built decades ago. Owners live in 68.7 percent of homes, and the typical value is $209,800. Households average 2.20 people and 23.2 percent of residents are 65 or older, so plenty of houses hold more room than their owners use.

The Gateway School District serves the municipality. The borough of Pitcairn sits entirely inside Monroeville near its south-southwest edge, so check the parcel record to see which municipality's rules and tax rates apply to a given address.

These are the figures buyers and appraisers tend to start from.

Housing measureMonroeville figure
Households, 2020 to 202412,634
Owner-occupied housing rate68.7%
Typical owner-occupied home value$209,800
Median owner cost with a mortgage$1,626 a month
Median owner cost without a mortgage$611 a month
Median gross rent$1,175

Owners without a mortgage pay little each month, so a long-held home can be cheap to keep and still need costly repairs. That is often when an owner starts weighing an as-is sale.

Monroeville requires a residential occupancy permit tied to the sale. An inspection has to be completed before the new owners move in. The fee is $100 for a single-family dwelling or townhome, and a second reinspection can add $50 under the municipal fee schedule.

The application works like this:

  • The current owner or the owner's agent files it.
  • It lists the property address, the buyer's name, who will meet the inspector and whether the electricity is on or off.
  • It has a line to mark the house as being sold as is.
  • The permit is issued in the name of the new owners who will live there.

The municipality's number is 412-856-3340. Call before you list so the inspection can be scheduled early, and leave the electricity on if you can. An inspector can't check the furnace, outlets or water heater in a dark house, and a second visit costs money and days.

sections.h2: If the house is a rental
sections.html:
Rental units need their own occupancy permit, and an inspection must be completed before a tenant moves in. The fee is $75 for multi-family units and $100 for a single-family dwelling or townhome, and the permit is issued in the tenant's name. Units occupied before inspection can face penalty fines under the municipal ordinance.

A tenant in place changes the sale. Ask the municipality whether the permit on file is current and hand that paperwork to a buyer who plans to keep the tenant. An investor who will rent the house after closing applies under the rental rules separately from the sale permit. If the tenant is moving out anyway, put the move-out date in writing so the sale inspection can happen in an empty house.

Monroeville sits at the higher end of the county table. The municipality takes 1 percent and the Monroeville-Gateway school district takes one-half percent. Add the state's 1 percent and the total is 2.5 percent of the sale price. The tax is paid to the county at the deeds office with its own check, apart from recording fees. Some family transfers are exempt, and form REV-183 covers deeds that show no price.

The charge appears on your settlement sheet in any sale, so request the exact total from the title company early. Who pays what is set by the sales contract, so read that clause closely before signing.

A challenge to your valuation starts with BPAAR, the county's first appeal level, and all of its hearings take place by phone. You can speak for yourself, send an attorney or appoint a representative. A losing party may carry the case to the Board of Viewers in the Court of Common Pleas.

The Gateway school district or the municipality can file an appeal against an owner too, and the owner is free to attend or skip those hearings. If you plan to sell, a lower assessment matters less than the price a buyer will pay, but it does cut your bill while you hold the house.

Start with a phone call to 412-856-3340 to learn what the occupancy inspector checks. Then pull together your lender's payoff figure, any lien letters and the parcel record. Decide between a listing, a cash offer and an investor purchase as is. When a contract is signed, file the occupancy form naming the buyer and book the inspection.

If the inspector marks problems, either repair them or write down who will pay for them. At the table you sign the deed, the county gets its transfer tax, and the title company settles your payoff before sending you the remainder. Mark the sale as is on the form and in the contract so the two documents agree.

Before you talk with a buyer, collect:

  • The address and the exact name on your deed.
  • Your lender and any other lien holders.
  • The power status, on or off.
  • Any tenant, plus the lease end date.

Speed depends on the inspection, the title and the buyer's financing. A cash buyer removes the loan approval step, but the municipal occupancy inspection still applies.

  • Order the occupancy inspection early and fix any items it flags.
  • Pull the county parcel record for the owner of record and school district.
  • Collect mortgage and lien payoffs, and leave the power on for the inspector.
  • Weigh a listing, a cash offer and an as-is investor sale against what repairs would cost.

With cash there is no bank appraisal or underwriting queue, the stage where financed deals most often slip. Closing day is short: you sign the deed, the title company clears the mortgage and any liens, and the remaining proceeds are yours.

sections.h2: Prepare the house and the commute pitch
sections.html:
Houses with outdated wiring, old roofs or deferred upkeep are the ones most likely to snag on the occupancy inspection, so walk through yours before a buyer does and note anything that looks unsafe. Small fixes done up front cost less than a delayed closing.

Monroeville sits where I-376, the Pennsylvania Turnpike at Exit 57, U.S. 22, Business 22 and PA 48 meet. Two Pittsburgh Regional Transit bus lines run to downtown Pittsburgh from park-and-ride lots here, and the Westmoreland Heritage Trail follows an old rail line to Trafford and Murrysville. A listing can highlight the commute, since buyers who work downtown weigh drive time heavily when they compare houses across the eastern suburbs.

faqs.q: What is the occupancy permit fee when selling a house in Monroeville?
faqs.a: $100 for a single-family house or townhome, with a possible $50 charge if a second reinspection is needed. The buyers can't move in until the inspection is done.

faqs.q: How much is the transfer tax on a Monroeville sale?
faqs.a: It totals 2.5 percent. The state takes 1 percent, the municipality 1 percent and the Monroeville-Gateway school district one-half percent.

faqs.q: Is Monroeville a city or a borough?
faqs.a: It is a home rule municipality. The area began as Patton Township in 1849, became a borough in 1951 and adopted its charter in 1974.
The Gateway School District serves students from kindergarten through grade 12. The county transfer tax table calls it the Monroeville-Gateway district.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Monroeville property assessment?
faqs.a: Yes. Go through the county's BPAAR board, which hears cases by phone. You may appear alone, use an attorney or name an authorized representative.
